messages.subject: Re: Item re-scored so that all values are within a distance of 1
messages.subject_clean: Item re-scored so that all values are within a distance of 1
messages.body_plain:
This means that there were unexpected spaces between responses, such as noticing the unique observations for a given item are [1,3,4,5]. The rescoring would change the observed values to [1,2,3,4] instead, and use that. The warning appears because for some models, like the rsm, this can provide the incorrect rating constraints and should be forced instead (e.g., see the customK input to the technical list). For other itemtypes though, this really isn't a big issue, and forcing the customK input for categories that were not observed could even make the model unidentified and fail to converge properly.

Phil

> On Wednesday, February 7, 2018 at 1:27:55 PM UTC-5, Phil Chalmers wrote:
> > The idea is that if the observed item's unique responses are of the form:
> >
> > c(1,2,4) == unique(item)
> >
> > where for some reason it's clear that the 3rd category was never endorsed, then mirt will change all instances of 4 to 3
> >
> > c(1,2,3) == unique(item)
> >
> > Hence, all the unique values are 1 unit appart. The reason is somewhat technical, but because IRT models assume categorical relationships the values of the coding scheme should be relevant, and this just helps the internal arguments determine the ordering and spacing of the categories. For most IRT models, such as the graded response, nominal, etc, this translation is irrelevant. For other models where the scoring scheme is meaningful (such as in a partial credit model) then the fixed scoring coefficients would need to be overwritten at the time of estimation. So, unless you are using itemtype = 'gpcm', then I wouldn't worry.

The large option has to do with minimization how long it takes to obtain the unique vectors of response patterns and their associated frequencies. This is a function of a few things, such as the sample size, number of response options, but more importantly the length of the test. For long tests there is a good chance that many of the responses observed are already unique, so this reduced table may end up having close to the same number of rows as the initial observation data (hence, it's really just time consuming to compute it). Larger sample sizes, even in the millions, may not be problematic if the number of unique responses is small due to using a shorter test with fewer response options.

> And while we're on the topic, other than changing the TOL and quadpts options, do you have any other advice for speeding up proc times?

Use Linux? I've noticed the estimation times are quite a bit smaller on Ubuntu than Windows 10 running the same hardware for some reason (maybe because everything must be complied on Linux and is therefore more efficient with the hardware, or it's just the OS itself that's better at computing). HTH.

I got it to work using the code below:

# Remove age column
newdat <- dat [,2:21]

# Make age into a separate vector
group <- c(rep('Early', sum(dat$age == "Age 18-30")),
           rep('Middle', sum(dat$age == "Age 31-49")),
           rep('Late', sum(dat$age == "Age 50+")))

# Specify theta, run multiplegroup
Theta <- matrix(seq(-6,6,.1))
mg <- multipleGroup(newdat, mirt.model('F1 = 1-20'), group)

# generate testinfo
tI <- map_dfr(1:3, ~{
  groups <- c("Early", 'Middle', "Late")
  ti <- testinfo(mg, Theta, group = .x)
  data.frame(information = ti, xAxis = Theta, se = 1/(sqrt(ti)), group = groups[.x], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
})

## print testinfo
print(tI)

messages.body_plain:
ltm reports the classical IRT parameterization by default; mirt uses the slope-intercept form. Both packages can be changed though (mirt post-estimation, ltm within the ltm() function).

library(mirt)

dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
mod <- mirt(dat, 1, '2PL')
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE)
coef(mod, simplify=TRUE, IRTpars=TRUE)

library(ltm)
ltm(dat ~ z1)
ltm(dat ~ z1, IRT.param = FALSE)

Phil
